comparator.name: International and European Law
comparator.sourceNotes: The first year is shared by both tracks. The International and European Law track continues with public international law, EU law and cross-border business law. It includes a required 30 EC exchange semester and a 10 EC thesis and oral defence.
components: Law and Legal Skills: the Dutch example
Introduction to Legal English and Research Skills
Introduction to International and European Law
Competition Law in the Digital Market
The Contemporary Value(s) of International Law

routeSelection.basis: The shared first year leads to two tracks. The International and European Law track provides the broader curriculum in the named field. Technology Law is a separate specialisation and supports the second UCR option.

core: International and European legal systems, sources, interpretation and institutions
Human rights, constitutional comparison, public power and judicial protection
Cross-border private, commercial, dispute and market regulation
Legal research, English argumentation and progressive academic inquiry
Law in political, historical and social context
adjacent: Technology law and regulation of digital innovation
International organisations, governance and political economy
questions: How do international and European legal orders constrain power and protect rights across borders?
How should law govern markets, cross-border business and disputes?
How should European and international law respond to digital innovation?

selection.assessment: The broad option gives priority to international, European and comparative law. The second option studies how digital technologies and institutions interact. International organisations, rights and market regulation are already represented in the broad option.

notes.text: UCR offers related study in international, EU, comparative and business law. Groningen gives dedicated attention to legal English, administrative regulation, judicial protection and digital competition law. The Groningen degree requires an exchange semester and a thesis with an oral defence.

alternatives.label: International, European and comparative law
alternatives.concept: Studies public international law, EU law, human rights and comparative legal systems. Courses in politics, history and social research help explain how legal institutions exercise power and how people challenge their decisions.
alternatives.labelReason: Legal systems, international law and constitutional comparison provide a foundation for EU law, private law and cross-border business law. Political and social research supports later study of public policy and conflict.
progression: Legal systems, international law and constitutional comparison provide a foundation for EU law, private law and cross-border business law. Political and social research supports later study of public policy and conflict.

alternatives.label: Law, AI and digital governance
alternatives.concept: Combines international and European law with programming, data systems and AI ethics. It examines how legal institutions and businesses respond to digital technologies and their effects on rights, markets and public policy.
alternatives.labelReason: Law and programming foundations support international and EU law, data management, networks and AI. Early ethics and data courses support later study of machine learning and digital business.
alternatives.distinctness: Programming, data systems, machine learning, AI ethics and digital business add a technical and regulatory focus.
progression: Law and programming foundations support international and EU law, data management, networks and AI. Early ethics and data courses support later study of machine learning and digital business.

courses: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: Develops academic writing, evidence appraisal and reflection in the first year.
Examines how AI affects market structure, business models, labour and corporate responsibility.
Applies comparative contract and trade law to cross-border transactions and examines intellectual property and commercial dispute resolution.
Uses industry cases and strategic planning to assess organisational responsibility and the effects of digital transformation.
Examines trade policy, international business institutions and corporate responsibility across borders.
Introduces how firms are formed, organised and financed, providing the business background required for Transnational Business Law.
Develops survey design, sampling, measurement and statistical inference for empirical studies of institutions and regulation.
Applies ethical frameworks to algorithmic bias, surveillance, interpretability and accountability.
Explains internet protocols, network architecture and operating systems relevant to telecommunications and cybersecurity policy.
Uses relational models, SQL and authorisation to organise data and control access to it.
Cleans, integrates and visualises data, building practical knowledge of how digital records become inputs to decisions.
Builds and validates predictive models, providing technical grounding for scrutiny of automated decisions.
Develops Python programming, testing and debugging to understand how software carries out decisions.
Introduces linear algebra, calculus and optimisation used in later machine learning.
Uses stakeholder research and policy evaluation to examine collective decisions, institutions and regulatory options in sustainability.
Uses comparative legal traditions, case-law research and moot court argument to introduce how legal systems operate.
Examines imperial administration, legitimacy and colonial rule to place legal and political institutions in historical context.
Applies rights frameworks, treaties and case law to questions about equality, dignity and state power.
Applies principles of criminal responsibility and defences through legal case analysis and a simulated clinic.
Studies treaties, jurisdiction and state responsibility through cases in public international law.
Compares separation of powers, constitutional rights, judicial review and administrative remedies.
Compares contract, tort and property rights and remedies across legal systems.
Applies EU institutions, competences, citizenship, internal market and judicial review principles to legal problems.
Evaluates normative arguments about punishment, privacy and equality that inform debates about legal rules.
Compares political institutions, constitutions and courts to explain how public power is organised.
Uses international-relations theory and simulated Security Council negotiations to examine cooperation, intervention and international authority.
Examines EU decision-making, legislation and interest representation from a political perspective.
Examines how policy is formulated across national and international institutions and develops evidence-based policy memos.
Examines international conflict, humanitarian law, rule-of-law responses and transitional justice in peacebuilding.
Uses sociological theories to examine inequality, social institutions and group relations, preparing students for empirical social research.
Designs qualitative inquiries and uses interviews, documentary evidence and interpretation to study institutions and their effects.
Uses environmental justice cases to study how communities organise and make claims in response to unequal harms.
Uses social theory and empirical civil-society research to examine public institutions, trust and collective action.
Develops structured argument, audience analysis and rebuttal for clear written and oral advocacy.
blocks: Both introduce legal reasoning and legal systems. Groningen uses Dutch law as its main example.
Both examine criminal responsibility and apply legal principles to cases.
Both examine treaties, jurisdiction, states and international institutions.
Both compare constitutional institutions, rights and judicial review.
Both study contractual obligations and civil liability. UCR also includes property law.
Both study EU institutions, competences, legal effects and the internal market.
UCR covers public international law and EU law in separate courses aligned to the more specialised Groningen components.
Principles of Private Law includes property and is aligned to Contract and Tort Law. Groningen gives property law separate coverage.
UCR covers constitutional and administrative principles. Groningen studies administrative law and market regulation together.
UCR covers cross-border transactions within business law. Groningen focuses on jurisdiction, applicable law and the recognition of foreign judgments.
UCR studies EU review and remedies within EU law. Groningen requires a separate course on judicial protection.
Groningen connects international relations theories to the values and interpretation of international law. The UCR international relations course is aligned to Law, Power and Politics.
Both use political science to study cooperation, power and international institutions. Groningen applies this approach specifically to the making and effects of law.
UCR studies empire and political institutions in historical context. Groningen provides a dedicated history of law.
Both study cross-border dispute resolution and arbitration. UCR includes this work within a broader business law course.
UCR combines AI ethics and computing with legal study. Groningen introduces technology law directly.
UCR studies international business and market institutions. Groningen gives market regulation dedicated attention.
UCR studies how AI changes markets and businesses. Groningen studies competition law in digital markets.
UCR develops written and oral argument across subjects. Groningen gives dedicated training in legal English and research.
UCR teaches social research methods. Groningen requires a seminar in legal research using legal sources and arguments.
The compulsory exchange comprises approved host courses, including at least 25 EC of law.
Groningen requires a thesis and oral defence. UCR independent research is optional.

audience.programmeDescription: The University of Groningen’s International and European Law degree studies legal systems and disputes that cross borders. The broad track focuses on public international law and European Union law.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR option combines law with politics, history and social research. The second combines law with computing and AI ethics to examine digital governance.

componentNotes.y3-exchange: Students complete 30 EC abroad, including at least 25 EC of approved law courses.
componentNotes.y3-research-colloquium: Students write and defend a thesis in English. Entry requires 90 EC of compulsory courses, all first-year courses and the Research Seminar.
